dataset.shortName: Fruiting trees and bird and mammal visitors
dataset.title: Fruiting trees and their bird and mammalian visitors and seed predators in the Anamalai Hills, India

abstract.para: This dataset includes occurrence records of trees, birds, and mammals recorded in the rainforests of the Valparai Plateau and the Anamalai Tiger Reserve in the southern Western Ghats, India. The data were collected between November 2017 and March 2019 as part of a study on plant-frugivore interactions and seed predation in fragmented tropical rainforests.

The dataset comprises 2641 records: 481 tree occurrence records belonging to 17 taxa (91.7% of records belonging to four focal species: Canarium strictum, Heynea trijuga, Myristica beddomei, and Machilus glaucescens) and 2160 animal occurrence records (1921 bird records of 23 taxa and 239 mammal records of 14 taxa).

Tree records represent individual trees selected for fruit-tree watches across a gradient of forest cover in forest fragments and benchmark (relatively contiguous) forests. Animal records represent birds visiting the focal trees recorded through visitation rate counts and focal scan observations, and mammals (primarily rodents and ungulates acting as seed predators) recorded beneath a subset of trees through camera trapping.

The data underpin two published studies. The first (Gopal et al., 2020, Biotropica) examined the effects of surrounding forest cover and fruit crop size on frugivory of four rainforest bird-dispersed tree species using the seed-dispersal-effectiveness framework to identify effective frugivores. The second (Gopal et al., 2021, Acta Oecologica) examined seed fates of the same four tree species, comparing seed predation by vertebrate and invertebrate seed predators between benchmark and fragmented forests.

geographicCoverage.geographicDescription: Rainforest fragments within Valparai Plateau and contiguous forests of the Anamalai Tiger Reserve, Tamil Nadu, India. The Valparai Plateau (220 km2, 10°15'-10°22'N, 76°52'-76°59'E) is dominated by tea and shade coffee plantations interspersed with over forty rainforest fragments ranging from 1 to 300 ha. The plateau is surrounded by the relatively undisturbed forests of the Anamalai Tiger Reserve (958 km2), Parambikulam Tiger Reserve, and Vazhachal Reserved Forests.

purpose.para: These data were gathered as part of the following Masters' dissertation project,

Gopal, A. 2018. Impacts of fragmentation on fruit removal and seed predation of four rainforest tree species in Anamalai hills, India. MSc thesis, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research, Mumbai, India.

description.para: Data from the two published datasets on Dryad (https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.5x69p8d0r and https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.qv9s4mwd5) were combined along with unpublished data on additional tree locations. Using R, these data were converted to GBIF Darwin Core format for upload.

The study was carried out within the Anamalai Tiger Reserve (ATR), Tamil Nadu, India (core zone: 958 km2, 10°12'-10°35'N, 76°49'-77°24'E) and the adjoining Valparai Plateau (220 km2, 10°15'-10°22'N, 76°52'-76°59'E) in the Anamalai Hills of the Western Ghats. The plateau has an undulating terrain from 600 to 1500 m elevation, receives approximately 3000 mm annual rainfall (70% during June-September southwest monsoon), and is dominated by tea (51%) and shade coffee (11%) plantations with rainforest fragments (4.5%) embedded within. Field surveys were carried out in rainforest fragments on the Valparai Plateau, benchmark forest sites within ATR, and some shade coffee plantations.

samplingDescription.para:
Field study was carried out between November 2017 and May 2018, with some additional camera trap monitoring extending to March 2019. 481 trees of primarily four focal species (Canarium strictum, Heynea trijuga, Myristica beddomei, and Machilus glaucescens) and 13 additional species were located across the landscape.
For a subset of trees (at least 30 per focal species, 131 trees total), birds arriving on the trees were recorded as visitation rates and focal scans through fruit-tree watches. Focal trees were watched for a minimum of five hours in the morning (starting from 06:00-07:30) and four hours in the afternoon (starting from 12:00-13:30). Two observers watched each tree using binoculars from 10-30 m distance. For each visiting frugivore, arrival and departure times were noted, and focal observations recorded fruit handling behaviour (pecked, swallowed, dropped, regurgitated, or removed).
For a subset of 29 trees across benchmark and fragmented forests, camera traps (Reconyx HC500 and Moultrie M-990i) were placed in seed plots beneath the canopy to record mammalian seed predators and their visitation rates. Seeds (10 per plot, marked with non-toxic marker and tagged with 50 cm Dacron fishing line) were placed in four 1x1 m plots per tree in cardinal directions to monitor seed fates.
In total, 2160 animal records were compiled (1921 bird records of 23 taxa and 239 mammal records of 14 taxa).

description.para: Trees, birds, and mammals were directly identified in the field by experienced observers using field guides cited in identification references. Taxa that could not be identified to species were identified to Genus or Family, or occasionally higher taxa. Species names were updated to GBIF taxonomy using the species name matching tool.

project.title: M.Sc. thesis project at the Postgraduate Program in Wildlife Biology and Conservation at the National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS), Bangalore, India

abstract.para:
This study is an M.Sc. dissertation project at the Postgraduate Program in Wildlife Biology and Conservation at the National Centre for Biological Sciences - Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (NCBS-TIFR), India.
Students who conducted their dissertation work in partnership with one or more of the Nature Conservation Foundation's (NCF-India) programs upload their dissertation data on GBIF as NCF is a GBIF publisher.
Dr Rohit Naniwadekar, Scientist, Nature Conservation Foundation, was a mentor and co-author of this study.

funding.para: This project was funded by grants from the Tata Trusts and core funding to the National Centre for Biological Sciences, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (NCBS-TIFR) from the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE), Government of India. Divya Mudappa and T. R. Shankar Raman acknowledge funding and partnership from Rohini Nilekani Philanthropies. Compilation and publication of this dataset was supported by Fondation Franklinia.

descriptor.name: generic
descriptor.descriptorValue: The study was conducted within rainforest fragments on the Valparai Plateau (220 km2, 10°15'-10°22'N, 76°52'-76°59'E) and contiguous benchmark forests in the Anamalai Tiger Reserve (958 km2, 10°12'-10°35'N, 76°49'-77°24'E) in the Anamalai Hills of the southern Western Ghats, Tamil Nadu, India. The plateau is dominated by tea and shade coffee plantations interspersed with over forty rainforest fragments ranging from 1 to 300 ha.

description.para: Four bird-dispersed rainforest tree species were selected: two medium-seeded species (Heynea trijuga and Machilus glaucescens) and two large-seeded species (Myristica beddomei and Canarium strictum). Trees were located across a gradient of forest cover. For the frugivory study, fruit-tree watches recorded avian frugivore visitation rates and fruit handling behaviour. For the seed predation study, seed fates were tracked in seed plots beneath trees using camera traps to identify mammalian seed predators.
